cards.title: Prawda/fałsz: jak sprawdzać zdanie
cards.body:
Dla każdego zdania znajdź w tekście **dokładny fragment**, którego dotyczy. Dopiero po przeczytaniu go decyduj.
1. TRUE – tekst mówi to samo, choćby innymi słowami.
2. FALSE – tekst mówi coś przeciwnego albo zmienia szczegół (liczbę, osobę, czas, miejsce).
3. Jeśli tekst o czymś nie wspomina, nie zgaduj z własnej wiedzy: w arkuszu odpowiedź zawsze wynika z tekstu.

cards.title: Parafrazy i zaprzeczenia
cards.body:
Zdania w zadaniu rzadko powtarzają tekst słowo w słowo. Szukaj **znaczenia**, nie tych samych wyrazów.
**Przykład:** tekst: "She has never travelled abroad." → zdanie: "She has been to many countries." = FALSE.
Uważaj na zaprzeczenia (not, never, no, nobody) i na pary przeciwieństw (win – lose, early – late, increase – fall).
cards.tip: Podkreśl w tekście liczby, nazwy własne i słowa never, only, all.

cards.title: Liczby i procenty w tekście
cards.body:
Teksty prasowe często podają statystyki, a zdania je przeformułowują:
**more than half** – powyżej 50%; **a quarter** – 25%; **a third** – około 33%; **one in five** – 20%; **almost / nearly** – tuż poniżej; **about / around** – w przybliżeniu.
**Przykład:** 41 procent to "fewer than half", ale "more than a third". Policz, zanim ocenisz zdanie.

cards.title: Słowa-pułapki: all, always, only, most
cards.body:
Wyrazy o skrajnym znaczeniu (**all, always, never, only, nobody, every**) łatwo zmieniają prawdziwe zdanie w fałszywe.
**Przykład:** tekst: "Some shops close at five." → zdanie: "All shops close at five." = FALSE.
Sprawdź, czy tekst naprawdę potwierdza to "wszystko" lub "zawsze". Wyrazy **most** (większość) i **some** (niektórzy) są łagodniejsze, ale też wymagają liczb lub słów z tekstu.

cards.title: Czas w arkuszu szkolnym
cards.body:
Arkusz szkolny trwa **60 minut** i ma **100 punktów** – to średnio około pół minuty na punkt.
Zadanie z tekstem czytaj raz uważnie, potem odpowiadaj. Zaczynaj od tych luk, których jesteś pewien, i wracaj do trudniejszych. Zostaw kilka minut na przejrzenie całości – w arkuszu można poprawiać odpowiedzi.

flash.front: Zdanie zawiera always, never lub all. Na co uważasz?
flash.back: To słowa o skrajnym znaczeniu: sprawdź, czy tekst naprawdę potwierdza "zawsze/nigdy/wszystko".

flash.front: Tekst nie wspomina o rzeczy z zdania. Co robisz?
flash.back: Nie zgadujesz z własnej wiedzy: odpowiedź w arkuszu wynika z tekstu.

flash.front: Ile czasu i punktów ma arkusz etapu szkolnego?
Co jest ważniejsze: te same słowa czy to samo znaczenie?
flash.back: Znaczenie – zdania są zwykle parafrazą tekstu.

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst, a następnie zdania pod tekstem (1–10) i zdecyduj, czy są prawdziwe (TRUE), czy fałszywe (FALSE). Za każdy poprawny wybór otrzymasz 1 punkt.
groups.text:
Pages, not screens: why teenagers are returning to paper books

A survey of 1,500 teenagers aged 13 to 17, carried out by Redfield Research, has shown that paper books are far more popular than many adults believed. On average, the teenagers questioned read three books for pleasure every year, and almost seven in ten of them (68 per cent) said they preferred a printed book to an e-book. Among the youngest group, aged 13 and 14, the figure rose to 74 per cent.

Why do young readers choose paper? The most common reason, given by 52 per cent, was that a book does not send notifications. 'When I read on my phone, I check my messages every few minutes,' said one fifteen-year-old. 'With a paper book, there is nothing to distract me.' Another 31 per cent said they simply enjoyed the smell and the feel of a real book, while 22 per cent liked being able to lend books to friends.

However, the survey also showed that e-books are far from dead. Almost half of the teenagers (46 per cent) had read at least one e-book in the past year, mostly while travelling, because a phone or a tablet is easier to carry than several heavy books. About one in five (19 per cent) said that they had listened to an audiobook, usually while doing sport or helping at home.

The biggest obstacle to reading, shared by 57 per cent, is a lack of time because of homework and after-school activities. A further 38 per cent admitted that they sometimes find it hard to choose a book, and 14 per cent said that books are too expensive. Librarians say that this last problem is easy to solve. 'Teenagers often forget that joining a library costs nothing,' says Helen Brooks, who runs a school library in Leeds. 'Many students are surprised when they find out that they can borrow up to ten books at a time.'

To encourage more reading, a number of schools have introduced ten minutes of silent reading at the beginning of every lesson. Head teacher Mark Davies says that the change has made students calmer. 'At first, some of them complained,' he says. 'Now they ask for their ten minutes if we forget.'

(Tekst i dane zostały wymyślone na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst, a następnie zdania pod tekstem i zdecyduj, czy są prawdziwe (TRUE), czy fałszywe (FALSE).
groups.text:
Every first Sunday of the month, the main street of Willowbrook, a small town in the north of England, belongs to pedestrians. Since 2019, no cars have been allowed in the centre between nine in the morning and five in the afternoon. The idea came from a local shopkeeper, Rita Osborne, who was tired of the noise and the traffic jams around her flower shop.

At first, many residents were against the plan. Café owners feared that customers would stay away if they could not park outside, and some elderly people worried that they would not be able to reach the market. The council therefore organised free minibuses from the car parks on the edge of the town, and promised to review the decision after one year.

The results surprised even the supporters of the idea. According to a council report, the number of visitors on car-free Sundays is 35 per cent higher than on ordinary Sundays, and the cafés earn about a fifth more. Street musicians, a children's bicycle race and an open-air book market now attract people from neighbouring villages. 'I thought I would lose customers,' admits café owner Dan Price, 'but I have never sold so many cakes.'

Not everybody is happy, though. Taxi drivers say that they lose money on those days, and one resident, Mr Clarke, complains that he cannot drive his disabled wife to the pharmacy. The council has promised to make an exception for such cases. Rita Osborne, meanwhile, hopes that the idea will spread. 'If a town this small can do it,' she says, 'so can a big city.'

(Tekst i dane zostały wymyślone na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst i wybierz poprawną odpowiedź na każde pytanie (A, B lub C).
groups.text:
Fourteen-year-old Zoe Bennett from Bristol has invented a lunch box that tells you when your sandwich is no longer fresh. The idea came to her last spring, after she found an old sandwich at the bottom of her school bag. 'It smelled terrible,' she remembers, 'and I thought: why can't a box warn me?'

Zoe spent three months testing small sensors that react to gases produced by food as it goes off. Her first experiments failed. The sensors she bought online were too expensive, and the cheaper ones gave the wrong results. Her older brother, who studies electronics, helped her find a better solution, but Zoe built the final version herself in the family garage.

The lunch box has a small light on the lid. It is green when the food is fresh, yellow when it should be eaten soon and red when it should be thrown away. In a school science competition, Zoe's invention won second prize. The winner was a group of students who made a bicycle light powered by the rider's movement.

A food company has already contacted Zoe. 'They were very kind,' she says, 'but I told them I'm not selling it yet. I want to improve it first.' Her next plan is to make the box cheaper, so that more families can buy it. 'My dream,' she says, 'is to stop good food from being wasted.'

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj uważnie tekst, a następnie zdania pod tekstem (1–10) i zdecyduj, czy są prawdziwe (TRUE), czy fałszywe (FALSE). Za każdy poprawny wybór otrzymasz 1 punkt.
groups.text:
Every summer, around two hundred volunteers climb the paths of the Eagle Mountains, but not to take photographs. They carry rubbish bags, tools and, sometimes, even young trees. The project 'Clean Trails' began eight years ago, when a mountain guide named Oliver Stone got tired of seeing plastic bottles beside the most beautiful paths. 'I counted forty-three bottles on a single walk,' he remembers. 'That was the day I decided that complaining was not enough.'

The first year, only twelve people joined him, mostly his friends and neighbours. Today the volunteers come from nine countries, and more than half of them are under thirty. Each group works for one week, sleeping in simple huts and cooking together in the evening. Participants do not pay for accommodation, but they must bring their own boots and a good sleeping bag.

The work is not only about rubbish. Volunteers repair wooden steps, remove dangerous stones and plant trees where the soil has been damaged by heavy rain. Oliver explains that one of the most important tasks is talking to hikers. 'People rarely throw rubbish on purpose,' he says. 'Most of them simply do not think about it. A friendly conversation works better than a sign that says: forbidden.'

Not everybody is enthusiastic, though. Some local farmers complain that the extra visitors leave the roads muddy, and a few hotel owners worry that tourists may stay away if the paths are closed for repairs. Oliver admits that these problems are real, but he believes that clean trails will attract more visitors in the long run, not fewer.

Last year the project received a small prize from the regional government. The money was used to buy new tools and to build a shelter for volunteers. Oliver's next plan is to organise a weekend for school classes, so that young people can try the work before deciding whether to join for a whole week.

(Tekst i dane zostały wymyślone na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)
